While I can't speak for all of them, I ised to be a carny. AMA.

Stories totally run the gamut. Everything from funny, to drama, to scary. I've gained a bit of a reputation with the company for not having a filter. Has nothing to do with being a carny, just from not giving a damn anymore. So my goal was always to make the other guys laugh, usually by twisted, dark humor. But the event that made me laugh the hardest personally actually didn't happen on a job. It was when we went for our inspector's licenses. There were four of us in this round of testing, and i'll use initials for the other parties. There were tons of other people, but only four from my company.

In my state, inspector's licenses require 3 eight-hour days of lectures followed by a test. Most of the lectures are about state laws, and there are some about horrible things that might happen if the inspector isn't doing his job. Safety is the number one issue, after all, so a lot of these lectures were very, very serious.

Day two of the lectures begins, and [K] announces to us that he had had several breakfast burritos and was beginning to feel the after effects of them. He spent the rest of the day farting on all of us.

Before I arrive for day three, I knew I would have to have my revenge. So I equipped myself with a rather gassy breakfast, and so did [K]. We begin the duel.

When we break for lunch, we discovered that they were serving baked beans as a side. It was buffet style, so I took my plate of food and one plate of beans. In an effort to intimidate him and the others, and as an excuse for levity, I ate them with my hands.

The game had been taken to the next level.

One of the last lectures of the day was called "fires and catastrophic events," so it was serious stuff. My group, in its infinite wisdom decided to sit in the front row. For the first 30 minutes, we farted on each other just naturally.

[K], who sat to my left, decided to up the ante, and break out a fart sound app on his phone. I could not keep my shit together. The guy is up there talking about the Magic Castle burning down in New Jersey killing 8 kids, and I'm laughing my ass off. I'm trying not to, but can't help it. [M] is sitting to my right, and can hear [K]'s phone, but thinks we're still playing legit. He asks in a whisper if it's me farting, and all I can do is shake my head no. Then he asks if it's [K]. I nod and try to compose myself.

[K], that fucker, kept his composure the entire time. It was the first and only time someone got me like that, because it's usually me trying to get everyone else to lose their shit.
That genuinely made me laugh. Thanks for replying, sounds like you have some good stories to tell :)

There's tons.

This one time, we were doing a truck show. Not sure why, but we were there. And we had a lot of different shit. The two pieces of import here are the zip line and the stunt jump. Mecahnically, the two are almost identical. A huge 25 foot stair case. The zip line, obvioisly, had cables at the top that ran down, the stunt jump had this giant, inflated bag at the bottom that you jumped into from the top of the stairs.

Both of these pieces require an operator at the top of them. So, I was on top of the Zip Line, and [A] was on top of the Stunt Jump. Both pieces faced the same direction, so the stairs ran parallel to each other and we're about 50 feet apart.

Because of the scale of this event, I had a walkie-talkie, [A] had one, and the boss had one in the ticket booth. Throughout the day, I was trying to make everyone laugh on the walkie-talkie. The fact that the boss had one, made [A] laugh even harder because he could hear what I was saying.

Things like "does anyone have eyes on that leprechaun? Tell [Z] he has to get him back in the cage before the end of the event. Don't let it trick him again!"

And, "we need to get that tarp for the donkey show. I'm looking at his balls, and I don't think he can wait much longer."

But that doesn't even begin to compare to what happened during lunch. Between 12 and 1, say, business was slow since most people were eating. I look over to [A] and he begins waving his arms in the air, which I correctly understood to be the opening salvo of an impromptu dance-off.

Now, neither of us are good dancers, at all, so the dances were all ridiculous. For a few minutes, we exchange moves. I then hold my palm above head level at arm's length and spit on it, then spank the invisible girl grinding on me (hard to explain without demonstrating).

Not over the walkie, but through the air I can hear [A] laughing from all the way over on his ride.

It was hysterical, because nobody saw us but each other. Or so I thought. [Z], the same kid who let out the leprechaun, told me later he was watching us. Figured we were communicating in dance. Like bees.

I had to think about this one. Nothing really scares me. The only thing that would usually unnerve me would be doing anything that would cost us money (through refunds from fuck ups or whatever). Usually, if everything is set up properly, safety isn't a huge concern anymore. Just as long as the kids aren't being assholes. They usually weren't. It's the parents that sucked. Invariably.

All mechanical bulls are basically the same. It's a base that has two motors. One bucks, the other spins. An inflated mat. And the bull itself. They make all kinds of shit that goes on the bases. They even make naked dudes, and the rope you hold onto is his cock, and naked chicks where the rope is her ponytail.

Anyway, we had this game that we for a time called "Wipeout." We actually got a cease and desist from Disney for calling it that. It was a mechanical bull base, but the mat was much bigger with four thick foam pads that are velcroed to the mat. Instead of a bull on top, it's a huge padded arm that spins in circles, dips, and raises. The players would stand on the pads and try to jump over or duck under the arm as it spun.

The arm itself was metal, I think steel. The pad that went over it wasn't a cored out cylinder of foam, but rather a cylinder with a lengthwise slit down to the center on one side. This means there's definitely a top and a bottom to it. First time it went out, we didn't know that.

The slit side of the pad was supposed to be in the bottom, but when we set it up, the slit was at the top. One, at first, might not think it matters. We certainly didn't. My ride is dead, so I'm watching the new one. I see this kid jump on the arm, then he and the pad fall off. I'm standing opposite the operator, so I see it first, the kid gets up facing me with blood pouring down his face.

Now, I'm thinking "that's it, the whole job is fucked. We're all in trouble." Fortunately, it was an ROTC academy, so these are the kinds of kids that have blood sports on the curriculum. Even the Commandant was like, "ah he'll just need maybe a stitch."

For that first hour after it happened before the commandant showed up was a little unsettling.

The only time I have ever gone to a fair or a carnival has been with a significant other and every single time I have gone to one, carnival barkers always try to exploit any (alleged) desire to defend my masculinity in front of the female that I have been with, while also making outrageously sexist remarks. For instance, a man running a high-striker will yell at me, "Come on, sonny boy, show that lady how it's done! Show her how strong those muscles are! Win your lady a prize!" and other things of this nature. Based on your own personal experience, is this as prevalent as my own personal experience has been? If so, are carnival barkers specifically trained to do this, or is it an attitude that is directly correlated with people who are attracted to this kind of work? Also, do you find that such approaches are even remotely effective? I always ignore these people, because the probability that such comments would influence me to spend money on these types of games is zero.

I'd love to know your take on this, in terms of being someone who has had so much exposure to the goings-on of the carnival scene.

I can't speak to its prevalence, aside from it being a stereotype. But, I can say that it does totally work.

I had a gig at some college somewhere (I can't remember where or which one,) and I was running this rope ladder climb. The ladders run at a very tight angle against the mat underneath. Maybe 25-35°, but there is a slight curve to them.

Anyway, these real built frat guys walk by, and I ask if they're interested in trying the ladders. Without stopping they all say no, and I troll them into trying with only nine words.

You didn't look like you had what it takes.

Well, that got their attention and all six of them attempted and failed to ring the bell at the top, much to my amusement.

Then this other time, a frat house in Troy, NY rented a mechanical bull. In my experience, there's always one or two people at an event that excel on the bull and will occasionally unlock what I always called "endurance mode."

I was always fair with bulls giving everyone the same ride, but the clock only went up to 99 seconds. So anyone who can hold on for 99 seconds, surviving all four pre-programmed difficulty settings was declared a champion. It was always amusing to me when someone scored a 30 or 40 and was very proud of themselves only to have me remind them that they still lost.

Anyway, this kid in Troy gets declared a champion and wouldn't come back to try again, this time with me controlling the bull randomly. I have to pack it all up and head to Jersey in about half an hour when I finally call over to him and ask if he's gonna try again. He declined, and I pulled out this gem.

I really like that shirt. It's a nice shade of bitch on you.

You could feel the atmospheric pressure change as the huge crowd of kids around the bull ring all go "Oooohh" at the same time.

He marched right back up to me, and to his merit, actually did manage to shut me up.

The difference between my job and the barkers at a carnival is that they're doing it to drive up ticket sales. Overwhelmingly, the majority of my gigs paid me the same no matter how many people climbed the ladders or rode the bull.

Also, you should know that most carnival games, high strikers included, can be rigged to be impossible.

Edit: missed a question

I know that I wasn't specifically trained to do it. I imagine it started in the 20's or so in an attempt to drive up ticket sales. Because there usually weren't tickets at my events, I did it out of boredom. But trolling is a skill i've mastered a long time ago.
